root_cause.text: In net/xfrm/__xfrm_state_delete(), xfrm_state hash nodes were unhashed based on mutable scalar fields (x->km.seq/x->id.spi) or without any unhashed check, so deletion could become inconsistent with the actual hlist membership and re-delete already removed bydst/bysrc/byseq/byspi nodes, causing use-after-free writes through poisoned list pointers.
root_cause.evidence: The commit states "__xfrm_state_delete() guards its byseq and byspi unhashes with value-based predicates" and that observing x->id.spi or x->km.seq outside xfrm_state_lock can be inconsistent with whether the object is actually on the list; it also notes "the bydst/bysrc unhashes have no predicate at all, so a second __xfrm_state_delete() on the same object writes through LIST_POISON pprev," and the patch fixes this by replacing hlist_del_rcu() with hlist_del_init_rcu() and checking !hlist_unhashed() for byseq/byspi.

intent_record.intent_summary: Fix xfrm state deletion to safely remove only hashed hlist entries and reinitialize their links after unlinking.
intent_record.what: The deletion code in __xfrm_state_delete() was changed to use hlist_del_init_rcu() instead of hlist_del_rcu() for the bydst, bysrc, byseq, and byspi hash-list nodes, and the conditions guarding byseq and byspi removal were changed from checking x->km.seq and x->id.spi to checking whether the nodes are currently hashed with !hlist_unhashed(...).
intent_record.how: At runtime, this makes state removal depend on whether each hlist node is actually linked rather than on related metadata fields, and it reinitializes the removed nodes after unlinking. This prevents deleting nodes based on stale or indirect conditions and reduces the risk of double-deletion or corrupt list state when a node is already unhashed or was never inserted.

grouping_result.intent: Fix xfrm state deletion to safely remove only hashed hlist entries and reinitialize their links after unlinking.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly matches the root cause: it makes xfrm state deletion remove nodes only if they are actually hashed and reinitializes links after unlinking, preventing inconsistent/repeated unhashing of bydst/bysrc/byseq/byspi entries that could lead to use-after-free writes.

candidates.rationale: This unconditionally deletes the bydst hash node without verifying that the node is still hashed, enabling repeated deletion of an already removed hlist node and causing list-pointer corruption/use-after-free writes.
Like bydst, this node is removed without any unhashed check, so inconsistent deletion state can lead to a second hlist_del_rcu on poisoned pointers.
Deletion of byseq is guarded only by the mutable scalar x->km.seq rather than actual hlist membership, so the condition can disagree with whether the node is hashed and trigger re-deletion.
Deletion of byspi depends only on mutable x->id.spi instead of checking hlist_unhashed(), allowing inconsistent removal and possible double-delete of an already unhashed node.
This conditional embodies the root cause by using a mutable scalar field to decide whether the byseq node should be unhashed, rather than checking actual list membership.

vuln_statements.explanation: This unconditionally removes the bydst hlist node without checking whether it is still hashed, so a repeated delete can operate on already removed/poisoned list pointers and cause use-after-free writes.
This unconditionally removes the bysrc hlist node without verifying actual hlist membership, allowing re-deletion of an already unhashed node and corrupting list pointers.
This conditional is part of the root cause because it uses the mutable scalar x->km.seq to decide whether byseq should be removed, instead of checking whether the hlist node is actually hashed.
This deletion is protected only by x->km.seq rather than actual hlist membership, so the code can attempt to delete byseq even when it has already been removed, leading to poisoned-pointer writes.

This removes the byspi node based on mutable state elsewhere in the function rather than an unhashed check, so deletion can become inconsistent with real list membership and trigger a second unlink of an already removed node.
